slide6.notes_script: From late August, two strands developed in parallel. While I worked on the standalone Graph rewrite and the Tree prototype, Kerk was designing the look of VisuAlgo+. My visualizers already worked, and their engines, editors and playback became the base of every later build. But each was a separate app with its own bars and controls, so they needed one page and one look. Kerk restyled visualgo.net into a design system: purple and gold, the Inter font, nine themes and twenty-six components. His UI kit recreates the home and visualisation pages, and the site I built later follows its home page. The kit's visualisation page is a scripted demo, though, so his design needed real visualizers behind it. Each strand filled a gap in the other. We carried forward three requirements: keep the drawing available, familiar playback across topics, and topic-specific information alongside. Kerk will now show how he laid out the visualisation page.

slide7.title: From nine wireframes to two working prototypes

slide7.step2_detail: By Kerk and Bao, after early student feedback that Kerk organised
slide7.step3_detail: Graph, Tree and Sorting in both layouts: his prototypes on Kerk's tokens and themes
slide7.band: Same features in both builds, so we could compare the layouts themselves on real runs, not just as drawings
slide7.wireframes_caption: Kerk's wireframes, 4 Sep 2026 · V2 and V7 outlined on the slide
slide7.builds_caption: Bao's working builds, 20–27 Sep 2026 (Graph shown, captured at ae63a62)
slide7.notes_script: Alongside the design system, I drew low-fidelity wireframes of the visualisation page, with an AVL tree as the example. I set one top bar and one footer for every version, with e-Lecture as a panel and a scrubber, zoom and shortcuts in the footer. They differ only in where the panels live and how they open. There are nine: seven layouts, plus V8 and V9, which show V7 during a drag and after the drop. I organised early feedback from students. It was formative input. After it, Bao and I chose two layouts together: V2, split rails, and V7, draggable docks. Bao then built Graph, Tree and Sorting in both layouts, from his standalone prototypes and on my design tokens and themes. That gave six working apps between 20 and 27 September. Both layouts had the same features, so any difference came from the layout itself, seen on real runs rather than drawings.

slide8.title: From V2 and V7 to V10
from_v2_points: Its panel positions as V10's default
from_v7_points: Panels moved by dragging their tabs
A bottom area and splitters to resize
credit_lines: Discussed together: Kerk and Bao, with Prof. Halim's feedback
Bao: built V10's panel-group model and shell (16–18 Oct)
Kerk: refined V10 with Bao and merged the apps into one (18–22 Oct)
slide8.footer: Left: Bao's V2 and V7 builds at commit ae63a62 · right: current app 346e84b, outlines added · captured 15–16 Nov 2026
slide8.notes_script: With six working apps, we could compare the layouts. V2 keeps every panel in a fixed place and lets several be open at once. V7 lets you move panels, but shows only one tab per dock. Bao and I discussed them, with feedback from Prof. Halim. In Week 9, we arrived at V10 to keep both strengths. Panels stay stacked and visible together, as in V2, and tabs drag between areas, as in V7. Each area can now hold several tab groups, and the canvas in the centre is never covered. Bao built the panel-group model and shell. I then implemented refinements we agreed on, such as drag sensitivity, controls and fonts. On 18 October, I merged the site and visualizers into one application with a shared layer, so a shell fix is now one edit. The Week 10 trial used V10. Bao will show the shell in detail later. Next, I will turn to the website and execution architecture.
